pageData.title: The Aghlabids
pageData.titleline: The Aghlabids - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Aghlabids were an Arab dynasty that ruled Ifriqiya, modern Tunisia and eastern Algeria, from 800 to 909. Nominally subject to the Abbasid caliphs of Baghdad, they were independent in fact, and their century of rule matters because it turned Kairouan into one of the great cities of the Islamic world and extended Muslim power across the central Mediterranean. Eleven emirs held the throne, beginning with the founder Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab, and their splendor was famous, though it was paid for with oppressive taxes.
pageData.para2: Their monuments still stand: the emirs rebuilt and enlarged the Great Mosque of Kairouan into the form visitors see today, and their vast reservoirs and water works, engineered to conserve and distribute the scarce rains, kept the country prosperous and mostly at peace. The emir Abu Ibrahim Ahmad in particular commissioned public works on a grand scale.
pageData.para3: It was at sea that the Aghlabids loomed largest. When the Arab soldiery rebelled, the emir Ziyadat Allah I turned their energies outward and sent them to conquer Sicily, beginning a struggle in 827 that left the island in Muslim hands for two centuries. Their fleet, supreme in the central Mediterranean, raided the coasts of Italy and France and made Ifriqiya a naval power to be feared.
pageData.para4: The dynasty's end came from within its own region: in 909 the Fatimid movement, preaching an Ismaili Shia rival to the Abbasid caliphate, overthrew the last Aghlabid emir and took his kingdom. Yet the century they ruled left a durable legacy in Kairouan's mosques, schools, and cisterns, and in Sicily's long Muslim chapter.
pageData.para5: Their reach kept growing: Aghlabid fleets took Malta in 870, and by 902 the last Byzantine strongholds in Sicily had fallen, leaving the island to a line of Aghlabid appointed governors. At home the emir Ibrahim II abandoned Kairouan for a new palace city at Raqqada, a glittering court that drew poets, jurists, and physicians from across the Islamic world.

pageData.title: The Almohad Caliphate
pageData.titleline: The Almohad Caliphate - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Almohads were a Berber dynasty that replaced the Almoravids in the 12th century and went on to rule Morocco, North Africa, and much of Islamic Spain. The movement began in the Atlas Mountains around 1120, where the reformer Ibn Tumart preached a strict but reformist theology built on the absolute unity of God, and in 1121 he proclaimed himself the Mahdi, the promised renewer of Islam. They matter because their empire was the largest the medieval Maghreb ever saw, and its monuments still define the skyline of Morocco and southern Spain.
pageData.para2: Under Ibn Tumart's successor, Abd al-Mu'min, the Almohads brought down the Almoravid state, capturing Marrakesh in 1147 and making it their capital, then sweeping east across North Africa. His heirs took Seville in 1172 and extended their rule over the rest of Islamic Spain, building the great Kutubiyya mosque of Marrakesh and raising Seville's Giralda tower in a style of rich Andalusian ornament.
pageData.para3: The empire reached its height under the caliph al-Mansur, who crushed a Castilian army at Alarcos in 1195. But in 1212, at the battle of Las Navas de Tolosa, a Christian coalition drawn from Leon, Castile, Navarre, and Aragon shattered the Almohad host, a defeat from which the caliphate never recovered. Ironically, the puritan movement Ibn Tumart founded became a golden age of thought: under Almohad patronage the philosopher Averroes wrote his commentaries on Aristotle and Sufi mysticism flourished.
pageData.para4: The empire fragmented in the 13th century as the dynasty retreated to North Africa: the Hafsids seized Tunis in 1236, the Abd al-Wadids took Tlemcen in 1239, and in 1269 Marrakesh itself fell to the Marinids. The Almohads vanished, but their conception of a united Maghreb, and their towers, gates, and mosques, endured.
pageData.source2label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Art of the Almoravid and Almohad Periods (ca. 1062–1269)

pageData.title: The Almoravid Dynasty
pageData.titleline: The Almoravid Dynasty - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Almoravids were a Berber Islamic dynasty from the Sahara that ruled Morocco and al-Andalus from about 1040 to 1147. They began as a reform movement among the Sanhaja tribes of the desert, the Lamtuna, Gudala, and Massufa, fired by the preacher Abd Allah ibn Yasin to deepen their practice of Islam, and they matter because for one remarkable century they linked West Africa, Morocco, and Spain into a single empire. Their wealth flowed from the camel caravans of the trans Saharan gold trade, whose routes the movement had first risen to defend.
pageData.para2: Under Abu Bakr al-Lamtuni and then the formidable Yusuf ibn Tashufin, the Almoravids conquered Morocco and western Algeria as far as Algiers between 1054 and 1092, founding their capital at Marrakesh in 1062. Yusuf took the title commander of the Muslims while still paying homage to the distant Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, and at home his scholars promoted a strict Maliki Sunni Islam.
pageData.para3: In 1085, as the Christian kingdoms of the north took Toledo and pressed south, the embattled Muslim rulers of Spain called the Almoravids across the strait. At the Battle of Zallaqa in 1086 Yusuf shattered the Castilian advance and halted the Reconquista for a generation, and soon the whole of Muslim Spain, save only El Cid's independent Valencia, answered to Marrakesh. Under his son Ali ibn Yusuf the union of Spain and Africa was consolidated, and Andalusian art and architecture flowered on both shores.
pageData.para4: Yet the Almoravids remained a desert Berber minority ruling settled peoples, and they could not restrain the tide of Christian reconquest that resumed with the fall of Saragossa in 1118. Weakened by rebellion and religious unrest, they faced a new puritan movement rising in the Atlas Mountains: the Almohads, whose armies took Marrakesh in 1147 and ended the dynasty.

pageData.title: The Byzantine Exarchate of Africa
pageData.titleline: The Byzantine Exarchate of Africa - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Byzantine Exarchate of Africa was a semi autonomous province of the Byzantine Empire centered on Carthage, established in the late 6th century by the emperor Maurice as a military command over the empire's North African territories, lands occupied largely by independent Berber peoples. It matters because it preserved Roman administration and Orthodox Christianity in North Africa for more than a century after Rome's western fall, and it served as the model for the theme system that would organize the whole Byzantine state.
pageData.para2: The exarch, appointed directly by the emperor, combined unlimited military and civil power in one office, and such concentrated authority could turn a governor into a rival. In 610 the exarch of Carthage sent a fleet under his own son, Heraclius, to Constantinople, where it overthrew the emperor Phocas and founded a new imperial dynasty.
pageData.para3: For decades the exarchate held the line: its armies and Berber allies repulsed the first Arab raids from Egypt in the early 7th century, and the brief revolt of the exarch Gregory around 647 showed how far Carthage's confidence still ran. But pressure mounted year by year as Arab armies pushed west, taking the exarchate's inland strongholds one by one.
pageData.para4: The exarchate fell to the Arab conquest in the late 7th century: Carthage itself was captured in 698, and its elites and churchmen fled to Sicily and Constantinople. North Africa then gradually became part of the Islamic world, though the exarchate's century of Roman rule left its mark in the region's churches, mosaics, and Latin speaking towns.
pageData.para5: The exarchate's story began with reconquest: in 533 the emperor Justinian's general Belisarius had taken North Africa back from the Vandals, restoring it to Roman rule after a century of Germanic occupation. Under the exarchs, African grain and olive oil once again flowed east to Constantinople, and Latin remained the language of government and church long after it had faded elsewhere in the west.

pageData.title: The Ethiopian Empire (Solomonic Dynasty)
pageData.titleline: The Ethiopian Empire (Solomonic Dynasty) - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Solomonic dynasty ruled Ethiopia from 1270, with interruptions, for more than six and a half centuries, one of the longest lived royal houses in world history. Founded by Yekuno Amlak after he overthrew the Zagwe kings, it grounded its legitimacy in a magnificent claim: descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, whose union, in Ethiopian tradition, produced Menelik I, the first emperor. It matters because under this line Ethiopia kept its independence, its church, and its identity through seven centuries of siege and change.
pageData.para2: The early Solomonic emperors expanded the empire deep into the highlands and defended Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity against the Muslim sultanates on their borders, chronicling their wars in royal chronicles that remain priceless historical sources. The greatest test came in the 16th century, when the armies of Ahmad Gran of Adal overran most of the empire, and only Portuguese muskets, and the death of Gran in 1543, saved it.
pageData.para3: After that near death, the dynasty rebuilt: emperors founded a splendid capital at Gondar, whose castles still stand, expelled foreign missionaries who pressed too hard, and weathered the great Oromo migrations that reshaped the horn. In later centuries central power ebbed into the era of warring princes, until the emperors of the 19th century, above all Menelik II, reunified and modernized the state and smashed an Italian invasion at Adwa in 1896, the victory that kept Ethiopia free when all Africa was being colonized.
pageData.para4: The dynasty's modern story is told in its own topic, but its arc is clear: through the reunifying emperors of the nineteenth century, the founding of Addis Ababa, and the victory at Adwa, the Solomonic line carried Ethiopia's independence, its church, and its identity into the twentieth century. The Solomonic legend, and the independence it guarded, remain at the heart of Ethiopian identity.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Solomonic Descent in Ethiopian History

pageData.title: The Fatimid Caliphate
pageData.titleline: The Fatimid Caliphate - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Fatimid Caliphate was an Ismaili Shia empire that ruled North Africa and later Egypt from 909 to 1171. Rising among the Kutama Berbers of Ifriqiya under the missionary preaching of Ubayd Allah al-Mahdi, it claimed descent from the Prophet's daughter Fatima and openly challenged the Sunni Abbasids for leadership of the entire Islamic world. It matters because it built Cairo, founded Al-Azhar, and for two centuries ran a wealthy state astride the trade routes of the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.
pageData.para2: From their first capital at Mahdia on the Tunisian coast, the Fatimids pushed steadily east. In 969 their general Jawhar conquered Egypt, and there the caliph al-Mu'izz built a new palace city beside the Nile: al-Qahira, the Victorious, known to the world as Cairo. Its great mosque of Al-Azhar grew into a center of learning that still thrives a thousand years later.
pageData.para3: At its height in the early 11th century, the Fatimid caliph could claim sovereignty over the whole of coastal North Africa, Sicily, the Hejaz and Yemen in Arabia, and southern Syria and Palestine. Fatimid wealth rested on commerce: their merchants drew the Indian Ocean trade away from the Persian Gulf and into the Red Sea, filling the ports of Egypt with spices, silks, and porcelain.
pageData.para4: Their power declined through internal strife and dependence on foreign mercenaries, and in the later 11th century real authority passed to the Armenian generals who commanded the Fatimid armies. Famine, faction, and Crusader pressure in Palestine hollowed out the state, until in 1171 the Kurdish general Saladin quietly abolished the caliphate and returned Egypt to Sunni Islam.
pageData.para5: Their rule left a distinct artistic world: Fatimid craftsmen produced lusterware pottery, carved rock crystal, and intricate woodwork prized from Spain to India. In Egypt the dynasty at first governed its Coptic Christian and Jewish subjects with broad tolerance, though the erratic reign of the caliph al-Hakim in the early 11th century brought periods of harsh persecution that later rulers worked to undo.
pageData.source2label: Humanities LibreTexts: 8.11: The Fatimid Caliphate
pageData.source3label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Art of the Fatimid Period (909–1171)

pageData.title: The Ghana Empire
pageData.titleline: The Ghana Empire - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Ghana Empire was a West African trading state that flourished from around the middle of the first millennium CE to about 1200, its earlier centuries still shadowy for lack of written records. It matters because it was the first great empire of West Africa: a Soninke kingdom that controlled the gold and salt routes between the Sahara and the forest zone, and whose fame as a fabulous land of gold spread across North Africa and into Europe. Its heartland, called Wagadu in oral tradition, lay in the grasslands between the Niger and Senegal rivers.
pageData.para2: Its capital, Kumbi Saleh, was one of the largest cities of its age: excavations show a town of mosques, a public square, walls, and a monumental gate spreading over more than a hundred acres. The Arab geographer al-Bakri described it in 1076 as a city ringed with wells and irrigated fields, its king attended by pages bearing gold-hilted swords and by the sons of vassal kings with gold plaited in their hair.
pageData.para3: The empire grew rich by taxing everything that moved: goods were taxed when they entered the country and again when they left. From the gold fields of Bambuk, kings enforced a famous monopoly: only the king could own gold nuggets, while merchants had to content themselves with gold dust, a policy that kept the metal's value high. Gold, ivory, hides, and enslaved people went north on camel caravans; salt, textiles, beads, and horses came south in return.
pageData.para4: Ghana declined from the late 11th century under drought, rebellion, and Almoravid pressure: the Berber movement sacked the capital around 1076, though evidence for a lasting conquest is thin. As trade routes shifted and the Sosso kingdom and then the Mali Empire rose, Ghana faded, but its legacy lived on in the states that followed, and its name was revived, centuries later, by the modern nation of Ghana.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Ghana Empire
pageData.source4label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Empires of the Western Sudan: Ghana Empire

pageData.title: The Hafsid Dynasty
pageData.titleline: The Hafsid Dynasty - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Hafsids were a Berber dynasty that ruled Ifriqiya, modern Tunisia and eastern Algeria, from 1229 to 1574, taking their name and legitimacy from the Almohad movement whose local governor, Abu Zakariyya Yahya, founded the line about 1229. They matter because under them Tunis rose to become a capital and one of the busiest trade centers of the Mediterranean, and because their three centuries made Ifriqiya a distinct and durable state.
pageData.para2: The founder kept the tribes in check and grew rich through trade agreements with Italian, Spanish, and Provencal merchants. His son al-Mustansir went further: he assumed the title of caliph himself, and for a time rulers from Morocco to Egypt acknowledged his prestige, the high point of Hafsid power. The dynasty also fostered the Maliki school of law, whose judges and scholars shaped the social life of Tunisia for centuries.
pageData.para3: The later centuries were harder. Already in 1270 the crusade of King Louis IX of France had camped before Tunis, where the king died of disease and his army withdrew only after extracting a tribute. Internal dissension, repeated Marinid invasions, and the depredations of corsairs wore the kingdom down, though rulers like Abu al-Abbas and Uthman restored order and prosperity for decades at a time. In these halls the young Ibn Khaldun, born in Tunis in 1332, began the career that would produce his famous history of the world.
pageData.para4: Caught between Spanish garrisons on the coast and Ottoman Turkish forces advancing from the east, the dynasty lost its independence piece by piece. A long struggle between Spanish and Turkish forces for control of Tunis ended in 1574 with Ottoman supremacy: the last Hafsid fell, and Tunis became a province of the Ottoman Empire.
pageData.source2label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Western North Africa (The Maghrib), 1400–1600 A.D.
pageData.source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: EBN ḴALDŪN, ABŪ ZAYD ʿABD-AL-RAḤMĀN

pageData.title: The Hausa Kingdoms
pageData.titleline: The Hausa Kingdoms - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Hausa Kingdoms were a family of city-states spread across the savanna of what is now northern Nigeria: Kano, Katsina, Zaria, Daura, Gobir, Rano, and Biram, the seven true Hausa states, ringed by seven outlying sisters. Never united under one ruler, they nevertheless shared a language, a culture, and a destiny, and they matter because their markets, crafts, and scholars made the central Sudan one of the busiest commercial regions of West Africa for five centuries.
pageData.para2: Each walled city was a world of its own, with its own king, its own specialties, and its own rivalries: Kano grew famous for its leather and indigo dyed cloth, Katsina for scholarship and trade, Zaria for its warriors and the slave raiding that fed its markets. The cities flourished through trade, crafts, and agriculture, their merchants carrying goods from the forest edge to the desert caravans and back again.
pageData.para3: The cities and their ruling houses were already centuries old when, from the 14th century, the kingdoms began linking into the wider world: Islam arrived with missionaries and merchants from Mali, and the new faith gradually took root in the courts and towns, though older beliefs lived on in the countryside. Because the seven states never combined, they often fell under the shadow of greater neighbors, Songhai to the west and Kanem-Bornu to the east, yet their cities kept growing richer.
pageData.para4: In the early 19th century the Fulani jihad swept away the old Hausa kings and organized their lands into emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate, and at the beginning of the 20th century the British took over the region as the Northern Region of Nigeria. Hausa culture never faded: today the Hausa language is one of the most widely spoken in Africa, and the old cities still trade, dye, and craft as they have for centuries.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Hausaland

pageData.title: The Kanem-Bornu Empire
pageData.titleline: The Kanem-Bornu Empire - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kanem-Bornu Empire was a long-lasting African state centered on Lake Chad, ruled by a single dynasty, the Sef, for close to a thousand years, from the 9th century to the 19th. It matters because no other African dynasty reigned so long: at its height the empire spanned lands that are now parts of Chad, Cameroon, Nigeria, Niger, and Libya, and it stood at the crossroads of trade between North Africa, the Nile valley, and the lands south of the Sahara.
pageData.para2: The empire emerged about the mid 9th century with its first capital at Njimi, northeast of the lake, and adopted Islam toward the end of the 11th century when its king, the mai Umme, became a Muslim, making Kanem one of the earliest Islamic states in Africa. Camel caravans carried salt, horses, and luxuries south across the desert, and slaves and ivory north, filling the royal treasury and equipping the empire's famous cavalry.
pageData.para3: The empire survived for centuries by adapting its capital and alliances: when the Bulala people drove the Sef from Kanem in the late 14th century, the dynasty simply moved west across the lake to Birni Ngazargamu in Bornu, and there it flourished again. Under the great mai Idris Alawma, who reigned around 1571 to 1603, the empire was extended and consolidated, its armies now armed with muskets and its court advised by Muslim scholars.
pageData.para4: It declined in the 19th century under pressure from the Fulani jihad that founded the Sokoto Caliphate, which drove the mai from his capital about 1808, and from the coming of European colonizers. The scholar-warrior Muhammad al-Kanami restored the state for a time, but the ancient Sef dynasty died out in 1846. Its legacy shaped the peoples of modern Chad, Niger, and Nigeria, where the Bornu emirate still endures.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Benin
pageData.titleline: The Kingdom of Benin - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Benin was a powerful forest kingdom of the Edo people in what is now southern Nigeria, flourishing from the 13th century until the British conquest of 1897. Ruled from its great walled capital by kings bearing the title oba, it matters because its artists produced the famous Benin Bronzes, brass plaques and heads ranked among the finest artworks ever made in Africa, and because its story shows a West African state dealing with Europe on its own terms for four centuries.
pageData.para2: The oba stood at the center of everything: he was considered to rule by divine right, he personally controlled all trade with outsiders, and he owned outright the kingdom's most precious goods, leopard skins, coral, pepper, and ivory. His palace, adorned with hundreds of brass plaques depicting warriors, courtiers, and kings, was the stage for rituals that bound the kingdom together. Under Ewuare the Great, who ruled from 1440 to 1473, the kingdom reached its greatest extent and the oba became an absolute monarch, advised by hereditary chiefs and by governors he appointed over the towns, the crown passing to the eldest son, a system that endured for the rest of Benin's history.
pageData.para3: From the late 15th century Benin traded with the Portuguese, who came seeking gold, pepper, and slaves and brought Indian cloth, cowrie shells, and brass in return. The oba bargained from strength: after 1516 he banned the sale of male slaves outright, needing the men for his own army, and the kingdom grew rich as the middleman of the forest trade.
pageData.para4: Benin's power faded during the 18th century as civil wars racked the kingdom and the coastal trade bypassed it. In 1897 a British punitive expedition stormed and burned the capital, looting thousands of bronzes that today fill museums across Europe and America, where they remain a symbol both of Benin's genius and of the unfinished reckoning with colonial plunder.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Benin
pageData.source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: 1.6.2: The Kingdom of Benin
pageData.source4label: BBC: What was the Kingdom of Benin? - BBC Bitesize

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Ife
pageData.titleline: The Kingdom of Ife - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Ife was a Yoruba city-state in the forests of southwestern Nigeria, flourishing from around the 11th to the 15th century, and it is revered to this day as the spiritual homeland of the Yoruba people, the place where, in their tradition, the world began. It matters because its artists created some of the most astonishing sculptures ever made in Africa, and because later kingdoms traced their kingship back to Ife.
pageData.para2: Ife's artists worked in cast bronze, brass, and terracotta, producing heads of such calm, naturalistic beauty that the first modern scholars to see them could hardly believe they were African. Their craft had deep roots: Ife's artists may have drawn on the traditions of the earlier Nok culture and of Igbo-Ukwu, whose bronze work was already astonishing in the 9th century. The faces, marked with fine scarification lines and crowned with beaded diadems, were probably portraits of Ife's sacred kings, the ooni, who ruled as the spiritual center of the Yoruba world.
pageData.para3: The city's influence reached far beyond its walls: in the traditions of neighboring Benin, it was the king of Ife who sent a master craftsman south in the late 13th century to teach the art of brass casting, and Benin's own royal line began with a prince of Ife. Scholars have not yet proven these connections by archaeology, but the shared symbols of kingship between the two cities speak for themselves.
pageData.para4: Ife declined as a political power when Oyo and Benin rose in the 15th and 16th centuries, but it never lost its sacred standing. Its kingship, its art, and its creation traditions remained the touchstone of Yoruba identity, and the ooni of Ife is still one of the most revered traditional rulers in Nigeria.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Ife
pageData.source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: 1.6.10: Kingdom of Ife- Sculptures from West Africa
pageData.source4label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Ife (from ca. 6th Century)

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Kongo
pageData.titleline: The Kingdom of Kongo - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Kongo was a powerful Central African state on the coast of modern Angola and the Democratic Republic of Congo, flourishing from the 14th to the 19th century. Born from an alliance of principalities in the late 1300s, it grew into the strongest power in west central Africa, ruling over two million people at its height from its hilltop capital, Mbanza Kongo. It matters because its story, of a sophisticated African kingdom that engaged Europe as an equal and was slowly consumed by the slave trade, is one of the great tragedies of the Atlantic age.
pageData.para2: Kongo was highly organized: a single king appointed provincial governors, who collected tribute of ivory, millet, and leopard skins at lavish annual ceremonies, and commanded a standing army of up to twenty thousand men. Its markets sold copper, salt, cattle hides, and its famous raffia cloth, and it even had its own money: the spiral nzimbu shells gathered from the island of Luanda, used like coins across the kingdom.
pageData.para3: In 1491 the Kongo king was baptized a Christian by Portuguese priests, and his son Afonso I, ruling from 1506, made Catholicism a royal faith, corresponding with the king of Portugal as brother monarch and sending his own son to be a bishop. But the partnership curdled: Portuguese traders, hungry for slaves for the plantations of Brazil and Sao Tome, ignored the king's laws, and the slave trade drained the kingdom's people and poisoned its politics.
pageData.para4: Kongo faced growing civil wars, Portuguese interference, and defeats by rival neighbors, and the old centralized state collapsed in the early 18th century, though its kings limped on in name into the 1800s. Its culture never died: Kongo language, art, and religious traditions survived the crossing to the Americas, where they echo still in the music and faith of the Atlantic world.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kongo

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Mapungubwe
pageData.titleline: The Kingdom of Mapungubwe - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Mapungubwe was a powerful Iron Age state at the meeting of the Limpopo and Shashe rivers, on the borders of modern South Africa, Botswana, and Zimbabwe, flourishing from about 1075 to 1220. It matters because it was southern Africa's first true kingdom: the earliest known state in the region, where social classes first separated, sacred kingship first appeared, and the foundation was laid for Great Zimbabwe after it.
pageData.para2: Mapungubwe's wealth came from its place at the crossroads: its herds of cattle fed the state, while gold and ivory from the interior passed through its lands to the Indian Ocean coast, bringing back glass beads and Chinese porcelain in exchange. Its rulers lived apart from their people, atop a great sandstone hill that served as both palace and sacred ground. The king was more than a chief: he was the wealthiest cattle owner in the land, bound in belief to the rainmaking on which the herds depended, and his wives lived in separate dwellings within his stone walled, palisaded court. At the kingdom's mid 13th century peak perhaps 5,000 people lived around the hill, while lesser chiefs ruled from smaller stone sites across the plateau as his vassals.
pageData.para3: The graves on that hilltop tell the story of a golden age: kings buried with gold bangles, beads, and the famous gold covered rhinoceros, a tiny masterpiece that has become the symbol of South African heritage. These treasures, unearthed by archaeologists in the 1930s, are today treasured as icons of the region's deep past.
pageData.para4: Mapungubwe declined in the 13th century as climate shifts and shifting trade routes drew power north to the Zimbabwe plateau, and its people became part of the rise of Great Zimbabwe. Today Mapungubwe is a World Heritage Site and national park, and its golden rhino stands as the emblem of the earliest chapter of South Africa's statehood.
pageData.source1label: Britannica: The Ancient Kingdom Hidden in Mapungubwe National Park
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Mapungubwe: The Great Iron Age Kingdom of Southern Africa

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Mutapa
pageData.titleline: The Kingdom of Mutapa - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Mutapa was a Shona state that rose in the 15th century as the heir of Great Zimbabwe, founded, tradition says, by a prince named Nyatsimba Mutota who led his people north to the valleys between the Zambezi and the plateau. Its kings bore the title Mwene Mutapa, lord of the conquered lands, a name the Portuguese heard and turned into Monomotapa, a word that glittered on European maps for two centuries.
pageData.para2: From its capitals in the northern hills, Mutapa controlled the gold trade of the plateau and the Zambezi valley, sending gold and ivory down to the Swahili coast at Sofala in exchange for Indian cloth, beads, and porcelain. At its height in the early 16th century the Mwene Mutapa was among the most powerful rulers in southern Africa, his court crowded with Muslim merchants and his armies collecting tribute far and wide.
pageData.para3: The kingdom's wealth attracted predators: Portuguese traders and adventurers pushed inland from Mozambique, meddling in successions, seizing trading fairs, and in the 17th century effectively reducing the Mutapa kings to clients. When the conquest came around 1633 it brought the Europeans disillusion: there was never as much gold as the legends promised, and terrible mortality from tropical disease soon drove them to abandon the far interior and concentrate on Mozambique. European dreams of a golden Monomotapa ended in disappointment, but the damage was done, as Portuguese pressure and internal division bled the state.
pageData.para4: Mutapa's power was finally broken late in the 17th century by the rising Rozvi kingdom of Changamire, which drove the Portuguese back to the coast and took over the plateau. The Mutapa state fragmented into smaller polities, but the Mwene Mutapa line endured in the east into the 20th century, and its history remains central to the story of Zimbabwe and Mozambique.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Mutapa
pageData.source4label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Eastern and Southern Africa, 1400–1600 A.D.

pageData.title: The Mali Empire
pageData.titleline: The Mali Empire - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Mali Empire was a powerful West African state that flourished from the 13th to the 16th century, the largest empire Africa had yet seen. Founded by Sundiata Keita, it controlled the gold, salt, copper, and ivory routes that crossed West Africa, acting as the great middleman between the Sahara caravan trails and the Niger River. The very name Mali, in the language of its founders, means the place where the king lives.
pageData.para2: Sundiata was a Malinke prince whose story is still sung by the griots of West Africa. Forging an alliance of chiefs weary of the harsh Sosso king Sumanguru, he crushed the Sosso at the battle of Krina in 1235, captured the old capital of Ghana in 1240, and was proclaimed supreme monarch by an assembly of tribal leaders and Muslim merchants. He set his capital at Niani, protected by mountains and close to the forests and waterways that fed the trade.
pageData.para3: The empire's most famous ruler, Mansa Musa, reigned from 1312 to 1337 and doubled its territory, governing through appointed provincial governors answerable to the capital. His legendary pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 showered Cairo with so much gold that the metal's price there crashed, and a generation later a European mapmaker drew him on the Catalan Atlas wearing a gold crown and brandishing a nugget. He brought home architects, scholars, and books, building Timbuktu's Great Mosque and the schools that made the city a byword for learning.
pageData.para4: Mali's power declined from the 1460s as subject states broke away, civil wars multiplied, and trade routes shifted elsewhere, while the Songhai Empire rose in its place. Yet Mali survived in a smaller form into the 17th century, and its memory never died: the epic of Sundiata remains the foundation story of the Manding peoples today.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Mali Empire

pageData.title: The Mamluk Sultanate
pageData.titleline: The Mamluk Sultanate - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Mamluk Sultanate ruled Egypt and Syria from 1250 to 1517, a state unlike any other in Islamic history: its rulers were slave soldiers, mostly Turks and later Circassians imported young, converted, and trained into an elite military caste whose members seized power and passed it among themselves. They matter because under their rule Egypt became the unrivaled political, economic, and cultural center of the eastern Arabic speaking world, and Cairo grew into one of the largest cities on earth.
pageData.para2: Their fame rests first on war: in 1260 the Mamluk general Qutuz smashed the Mongol army at Ain Jalut in Palestine, the first major defeat the Mongol empire could not avenge, and saved Egypt and the Islamic heartlands from conquest. Soon after, Baybars seized the throne and went on to break the remaining Crusader strongholds in Palestine and Syria, expelling the Crusaders from the mainland for good.
pageData.para3: The sultans made Cairo magnificent: they reestablished the Abbasid caliphate there in 1261, sheltering a claimant from the ruins of Mongol-sacked Baghdad, and lavished the city with mosques, madrasas, and markets. Merchants grown rich on the Red Sea spice trade filled its bazaars, and scholars made it the intellectual capital of Islam. Under the long reign of al-Nasir, who concluded a lasting truce with the Mongols in 1323, the state reached its prosperous height.
pageData.para4: Their economy and military declined after the 15th century as plague, factional strife, and the Portuguese intrusion into the Indian Ocean cut into the spice revenues. The rising Ottoman Empire defeated the Mamluks in 1516 and 1517, and Egypt became an Ottoman province, though the Mamluk caste itself endured in Egyptian life for centuries more.
pageData.source2label: Humanities LibreTexts: 8.13: The Mamluk Sultanate
pageData.source3label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Art of the Mamluk Period (1250–1517)

pageData.title: The Marinid Sultanate
pageData.titleline: The Marinid Sultanate - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Marinids were a Zenata Berber dynasty that ruled Morocco from 1244 to 1465, heirs to the wreckage of the Almohad empire. Established in eastern Morocco for generations, they rose under their chief Abu Yahya, who captured Fez in 1248 and made it the Marinid capital, and under Abu Yusuf Ya'qub, who took Marrakesh from the last Almohads in 1269 and became master of Morocco. They matter because they made Fez one of the great cities of the Islamic world and fought the last great Moroccan campaigns in Spain.
pageData.para2: Fez flowered under their patronage: the sultans founded a belt of madrasas, colleges of law and theology, whose carved courtyards remain among the glories of Moroccan art, and the city's scholars, merchants, and crafts made it the intellectual capital of the Maghreb. Art, scholarship, and trade all thrived under Marinid rule.
pageData.para3: The Marinids declared jihad in Spain and campaigned there until the mid 14th century, helping the Nasrid kingdom of Granada hold its ground and slowing the Christian advance toward the Strait of Gibraltar, though they recaptured no lost territory. Their greatest sultan, Abu al-Hasan, seized Tlemcen in 1337 and briefly reunited much of the Maghreb, but neither he nor his successor Abu Inan could break Hafsid rule in Tunisia, and the endless campaigns depleted the dynasty's strength. The disaster came at the Battle of Rio Salado in 1340, where a Castilian-Portuguese army destroyed the Marinid host and ended Moroccan power in Spain for good; Abu Inan was murdered by his own vizier in 1358, and the sultanate slid toward anarchy.
pageData.para4: Their power declined through internal factions and, in the 15th century, Portuguese attacks on the coast, beginning with the fall of Ceuta in 1415. In 1465 a collateral branch, the Wattasids, took over what remained, and Morocco entered a long struggle with growing European pressure along its shores.
pageData.source1label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Western North Africa (The Maghrib), 1000–1400 A.D.
pageData.source2label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: DELHI SULTANATE
pageData.source3label: Smithsonian Magazine: The Moroccan Sultan Who Protected His Country's Jews During World War II

pageData.title: The Songhai Empire
pageData.titleline: The Songhai Empire - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Songhai Empire was a major West African state centered on the bend of the Niger River, the last and largest of the great Sudanese empires. It flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries under rulers like Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad, who welded the river cities of Gao, Timbuktu, and Djenne into a single realm. It matters because it carried the West African tradition of empire, trade, and scholarship to its height before gunpowder weapons reached the desert's edge.
pageData.para2: Sunni Ali, who ruled from 1464 to 1492, built the empire by force of arms: his armored cavalry and river canoe fleet took Timbuktu in 1468 and starved Djenne into surrender, while his reputation as a ruler of uncanny powers kept subjects in awe. After his death his general Askia Muhammad seized the throne in 1493, founding a new dynasty and giving the empire its most celebrated government.
pageData.para3: Askia Muhammad reorganized the realm into provinces under appointed governors, standardized weights and measures, and made a grand pilgrimage to Mecca that announced Songhai's wealth to the wider Islamic world. Timbuktu itself had been founded around 1100 by Tuareg nomads, where the bend of the Niger met the starting point of the trans-Saharan caravans, and through it flowed ivory, textiles, horses, glassware, weapons, sugar, and kola nuts. Under his rule Timbuktu became a center of Islamic learning and trade at its peak: the scholars of the Sankore quarter taught law, astronomy, and medicine, and the city's book trade was its most famous industry.
pageData.para4: The empire fell with stunning speed: in 1591 a Moroccan expedition armed with muskets crossed the Sahara and shattered the Songhai host at the battle of Tondibi. Its collapse fragmented the region; smaller states and local trade networks replaced the old empire, and the Niger bend never again saw a power of its scale.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Songhai Empire

pageData.title: The Sultanate of Adal
pageData.titleline: The Sultanate of Adal - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Sultanate of Adal was a Muslim state of the Horn of Africa, centered in the Danakil and Somali lowlands with its capital at the walled city of Harar. It matters because for one blazing generation in the 16th century it came within a hairs breadth of conquering the ancient Christian empire of Ethiopia, a war that drew both the Ottoman and Portuguese empires into the Horn.
pageData.para2: Adal's rivalry with Ethiopia began in the 14th century with border raids and skirmishes, but under the governor Mahfuz the raids grew into open war, until he was killed in an Ethiopian ambush in 1516. His successor was one of the great war leaders of African history: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim, called Gran, the left handed, who rallied the Muslim nomads for jihad.
pageData.para3: Gran's armies swept into the highlands, destroyed churches and monasteries, drove the Ethiopian emperor into mountain exile, and by 1533 controlled most of central Ethiopia. Where his armies ruled, conversions were forced on a massive scale. The fugitive emperor appealed to Portugal, and 400 Portuguese musketeers landed at Massawa on the Red Sea coast in 1541, while Adal reinforced with 900 Turkish, Arab, and Albanian musketeers and cannon of its own, making the Horn an early battlefield of the gunpowder age.
pageData.para4: The tide turned at a battle near Lake Tana in 1543, where Gran was killed; his army dissolved almost overnight, and Ethiopia, with Portuguese help, reclaimed its highlands. Adal fragmented, its rulers eventually fleeing into the desert as Oromo migrations swept the region, but the sultanate's wars left a lasting legacy in the spread of Islam across the Horn and in the walls of Harar, still standing today.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Abyssinia

pageData.title: The Swahili Coast City-States (Kilwa, Mombasa, etc.)
pageData.titleline: The Swahili Coast City-States (Kilwa, Mombasa, etc.) - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Swahili Coast city-states were a chain of trading towns strung along the shores and islands of East Africa, from Mogadishu in the north to Kilwa in the south, including Mombasa, Zanzibar, and many more. They flourished from the 10th to the 15th century through Indian Ocean trade, and they matter because they created something entirely new: a culture and a language blending African roots with Arab, Persian, and Indian influences, whose name, Swahili, comes simply from the Arabic word for coast.
pageData.para2: From the mid 8th century Muslim merchants from Arabia settled in the coastal towns, joined in the 12th century by settlers from Persia, and their intermarriage with the local Bantu peoples produced the Swahili world: Islamic in faith, African in tongue, and turned toward the sea. The Swahili language, a Bantu language enriched with Arabic words, became the lingua franca of East Africa and is spoken by millions today.
pageData.para3: The cities grew rich as the gateway between Africa's interior and the ocean world: gold and ivory from as far south as Great Zimbabwe passed through Kilwa's emporium at Sofala, while goods from Arabia, India, and even China flowed back. Kilwa minted its own coins, and its sultans built in coral stone: the Great Mosque and the vast Husuni Kubwa palace, its walls studded with Chinese porcelain, so impressed the traveler Ibn Battuta in 1331 that he called Kilwa one of the most beautiful towns in the world.
pageData.para4: The arrival of the Portuguese around 1500 shattered this world: their fortresses at Sofala and Mozambique Island, and their policy of seizing trade by cannon rather than competing for it, drove the caravan routes north and ended the coast's golden age. Some city-states carried on under the Omani Empire into the 18th century, but the heyday of the independent Swahili towns was over.
pageData.source2label: Humanities LibreTexts: 9.9: The Swahili City-States (East Africa)
pageData.source4label: National Geographic: Kilwa, the abandoned East African city, once controlled the medieval gold trade

pageData.title: The Zagwe Dynasty
pageData.titleline: The Zagwe Dynasty - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Zagwe Dynasty ruled the highlands of Ethiopia from about 1137 to 1270, a line of kings from the Agaw people who took the throne from the last heirs of ancient Aksum. They matter because their century and a half produced one of the wonders of the medieval world: the rock hewn churches of Lalibela, whole buildings carved downward into living stone.
pageData.para2: The Zagwe kings moved their capital to Roha, safe in their native Lasta Mountains, and won the church's blessing for their shaky claim to the crown by showering it with royal endowments. Their claim rested on a legendary marriage to a daughter of one of the last Aksumite kings, and their writ ran over much of northern and central Ethiopia, though the hill country east of the Shewa Plateau slipped away to rising Muslim states such as Ifat and Hadya. Their faith was not quiet piety: they combined a hard, mobile military life with a burning desire to build monuments to Christianity, and their realm kept Ethiopia Christian while Muslim states rose on its eastern flank.
pageData.para3: The dynasty's crowning glory came under King Lalibela at the start of the 13th century: eleven monolithic churches, cut from the rock of his capital so perfectly that tradition holds angels worked beside the masons by night. The town was later renamed for him, and the churches remain a living place of pilgrimage eight centuries on.
pageData.para4: The Zagwe were overthrown around 1270 by Yekuno Amlak, an Amhara prince whose rebellion drove out and killed the last Zagwe king, founding the Solomonic dynasty, which claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Later church tradition smoothed the usurpation into a willing abdication, but the Zagwe legacy, in stone and faith, needed no smoothing.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Abyssinia
pageData.source4label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Eastern and Southern Africa, 1000–1400 A.D.

pageData.title: Zimbabwe
pageData.titleline: Zimbabwe - The History Web
pageData.para1: Great Zimbabwe was a major medieval city and trading state in southeastern Africa, flourishing from about 1100 to 1450 as the capital of a Shona kingdom. It matters because its stone walls and towers, raised from granite blocks without a drop of mortar, are the largest ancient structures in sub Saharan Africa, proof, for a world that once doubted it, that medieval Africa built civilizations of the first rank.
pageData.para2: The very word zimbabwe means houses of stone, and the greatest of them, the Great Enclosure, wraps a space 250 meters around in walls up to eleven meters high, guarding a mysterious conical tower. Kings ruled from the hilltop citadel above, and the finest treasures, gold bangles, imported glass and Chinese porcelain, and the famous soapstone birds, were buried in these royal precincts. Clusters of such stone buildings, zimbabwe in the Bantu tongue, gave both the city and the kingdom their name.
pageData.para3: The city's wealth came from the land and the long trade: cattle and farming fed it, gold from the plateau mines enriched it, and caravans carried gold and ivory to the Swahili coast, where ships took them to Arabia, Persia, India, and China. At its height perhaps twenty thousand people lived in and around the stone walls.
pageData.para4: Great Zimbabwe was abandoned in the 15th century, probably as its gold gave out and its fields could no longer feed its people, and the Shona rulers moved north to found new powers like Mutapa. But its memory endured: the soapstone bird found in its ruins flies today on the flag of Zimbabwe, the modern nation that took its name, and its pride, from these stones.
pageData.source2label: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Great Zimbabwe National Monument

pageData.title: The Idrisid Dynasty
pageData.titleline: The Idrisid Dynasty - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Idrisid Dynasty. The Idrisid dynasty (788-974) founded the first great Moroccan state and made Fez one of the leading cities of the Islamic world. Its founder, Idris ibn Abdallah, was a great-grandson of the Prophet Muhammad's grandson Hasan who fled east after his family was defeated by the Abbasid caliphs. Reaching the far Maghreb in 788, he won the allegiance of Berber tribes near the ancient Roman city of Volubilis, where local notables proclaimed him their leader, laying the foundations of an independent Moroccan kingdom.
pageData.para2: Poisoned by an Abbasid agent in 791, Idris I left a posthumous son, Idris II, who was raised among the Berbers and proclaimed ruler as a boy. Idris II made the dynasty's fortune: he moved his capital to Fez in 808, and the young city grew rapidly as waves of Arab immigrants arrived, including thousands of families from Kairouan in Ifriqiya and from Cordoba in al-Andalus, who settled in their own quarters and brought crafts, learning, and commerce. The Qarawiyyin mosque, founded in this era, became one of the great centers of scholarship in the Muslim world.
pageData.para3: Under Idris II's sons the realm was divided among princes of the family, and Idrisid rule stretched across much of northern Morocco and into what is now Algeria. The dynasty balanced between the great powers of the age, the Umayyads of Cordoba and the Fatimids of Ifriqiya, both of whom sought control of the Maghreb. That balancing act eventually failed: caught between the two rivals, the Idrisids lost their independence in the tenth century, and the last members of the family were killed or driven out by 974.
pageData.para4: The Idrisids left an enduring legacy out of proportion to their two centuries of power. They established the principle of an independent Moroccan monarchy, they implanted Arab-Islamic urban culture in the Maghreb, and above all they founded Fez, whose old city remains one of the best-preserved medieval urban landscapes in the world. Later Moroccan dynasties honored their memory, and the tomb of Idris II in Fez is still venerated as the shrine of the city's founder.
pageData.source1label: Maroc.ma: The Founding of Fez by Idris I and Idris II
pageData.source2label: Encyclopedie Berbere: Idris Ier

pageData.title: The Rustamid Imamate
pageData.titleline: The Rustamid Imamate - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Rustamid Imamate. The Rustamid imamate (777-909) was the first important Islamic state of the central Maghreb, ruled from the city of Tahert in what is now Algeria. It was founded by Abd al-Rahman ibn Rustam, a Persian-born scholar who had studied under the early leaders of the Ibadi movement in Basra. After Ibadi uprisings against the Abbasids failed in the east, Ibn Rustam fled west, and in 777 the Ibadi communities of the region elected him imam, establishing a state independent of the caliphate.
pageData.para2: The imamate was organized around Ibadi religious principles. The imam was chosen for piety and learning rather than pure hereditary right, advised by councils of religious scholars, and expected to live simply. Tahert grew into a handsome and prosperous city surrounded by gardens and fortified walls, home to Berber tribes of the region, Arab settlers, and merchants and scholars from across the Islamic world, including Christians and Jews who lived under its protection. Ibadi missionaries and traders spread the doctrine from Tahert deep into the Sahara and the Sudan.
pageData.para3: Tahert owed much of its wealth to trade. The city sat on the routes linking the Mediterranean coast with the oases of the northern Sahara, and its merchants dealt in goods moving between Ifriqiya, al-Andalus, and the regions beyond the desert. Contemporary writers described Tahert as one of the most flourishing towns of the Maghreb, and its imams maintained diplomatic relations with their nominal Abbasid overlords while in practice governing themselves for over a century.
pageData.para4: The end came with the rise of the Fatimids. The Fatimid movement conquered Ifriqiya in 909 and then swept west; Tahert was taken, the last Rustamid imams were killed or fled, and surviving Ibadi communities retreated to desert strongholds such as the Mzab valley, where they remain today. The Rustamid imamate is remembered as a pioneering experiment in elected religious government, and as the state that carried Islamic urban civilization into the central Maghreb a generation before the rise of Fez.
pageData.source1label: Al-Masaq (Taylor & Francis): Identifying the Rustamid Imamate
pageData.source2label: Amazigh History: The Rustamids and Ibadi Networks

pageData.title: The Zirid and Hammadid Dynasties
pageData.titleline: The Zirid and Hammadid Dynasties - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Zirid and Hammadid Dynasties. The Zirid and Hammadid dynasties (973-1152) were Berber ruling houses of the Sanhaja confederation who governed Ifriqiya and the central Maghreb, roughly modern Tunisia and eastern Algeria, between the age of the Fatimids and that of the Almohads. The Zirids rose as Fatimid governors: when the Fatimid caliphs moved east to their new conquest of Egypt in 973, they left their trusted Sanhaja commander Buluggin ibn Ziri to rule Ifriqiya in their name, and his descendants soon behaved as independent sovereigns.
pageData.para2: The Zirid century saw both splendor and catastrophe. From their base at Kairouan the Zirid amirs built palaces and patronized learning, and the dynasty's great royal cities included al-Mansuriyya and, later, Mahdia on the coast. In 1049 the Zirids finally broke with the Fatimids and transferred their allegiance to the Abbasid caliph. The Fatimids answered by unleashing the Arab Bedouin tribes of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym on Ifriqiya. The Hilalian migrations transformed the countryside, accelerated the Arabization of the Maghreb, and shattered Zirid power; Kairouan was sacked in 1057 and the Zirids withdrew to their coastal cities.
pageData.para3: The western branch of the family fared better. In 1007 a split had given the central Maghreb to the Hammadids, relatives of the Zirids, who built two of the most remarkable fortified cities of the medieval Islamic world: Ashir and, from 1007, the Qalaa of the Banu Hammad, a mountain capital whose ruined mosque tower and palace complex are now a World Heritage site. The Hammadids prospered on trade and diplomacy until they too were weakened by the Hilalian tribes and finally absorbed by the Almohads in 1152.
pageData.para4: Together the two dynasties carried Berber political power to its height in the medieval Maghreb. They defended the region against the Zanata rivals of the west and the Normans of Sicily, who briefly seized Mahdia from the Zirids in 1148. Their era bridges the age of the caliphates and that of the great Berber empires, and their surviving monuments at Kairouan, Mahdia, Ashir, and the Qalaa remain among the finest witnesses of medieval North African civilization.
pageData.source1label: Qantara: The Zirids and the Hammadids
pageData.source2label: Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Maghrib, 1000-1400 A.D.

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Takrur
pageData.titleline: The Kingdom of Takrur - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Takrur. The kingdom of Takrur (c. 800-1286) was one of the earliest known states of West Africa and the first in the region whose rulers embraced Islam. It lay in the middle valley of the Senegal River, in the land the Fulani call Futa Toro, and Arabic geographers such as al-Bakri described it as a powerful kingdom whose people were black Muslims, remarkable at a time when Islam had barely crossed the Sahara. Takrur's merchants traded gold, brought from the Bambuk fields further south, for salt and goods carried by desert caravans.
pageData.para2: The kingdom's defining moment came in the eleventh century. Around 1030 its king, War Jabi, accepted Islam and made it the religion of his court and people, one of the first royal conversions in sub-Saharan Africa. When the Almoravid movement arose among the Sanhaja of the western Sahara, Takrur became one of its earliest allies; King War Jabi's son joined the Almoravids in their campaigns, and Takruri soldiers fought in the armies that conquered Morocco and crossed into Spain. Arabic sources of the period sometimes used the name Takrur so broadly that it stood for the whole of the Western Sudan.
pageData.para3: Takrur remained a significant power into the thirteenth century, controlling the river trade and ruled by the Manna dynasty, but the rise of the Mali Empire ended its independence. Sundiata's successors expanded west toward the Senegal, and by about 1286 Takrur had been absorbed into Mali, its lands becoming the empire's western provinces. Centuries later the region re-emerged under Fulani rule, and the old name survived in Arabic writing as a word for the people of the Sudan.
pageData.para4: Takrur matters out of proportion to the scanty records it left. It shows that organized kingdoms with Muslim courts existed in West Africa centuries before the famous empires of Mali and Songhai, and it stood at the meeting point of the river, the gold fields, and the desert routes that made West African trade possible. Historians still debate its exact borders and history, but its place among the founding states of the Western Sudan is secure.
pageData.source2label: Brill Encyclopaedia of Islam: Takrur
pageData.source3label: Yale University Press: The Search for Takrur
pageData.source4label: Journal of African History: Takrur: The History of a Name

pageData.title: The Za Dynasty of Gao
pageData.titleline: The Za Dynasty of Gao - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Za Dynasty of Gao. The Za dynasty of Gao (c. 690-1335) ruled the first kingdom of the Songhay people, centuries before the famous Songhai Empire of Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad. The Songhay lived along the middle Niger, and their chief town, Gao, grew rich on trade between the river and the desert. According to the great Songhay chronicle, the Tarikh al-Sudan, the Za line was founded by Za al-Yaman, a stranger said to have come from the east, whose descendants ruled Gao as kings for generations.
pageData.para2: Gao's kings profited from the trans-Saharan gold trade and from their command of the Niger. Arabic writers knew the town as Kawkaw and described it as one of the great markets of the Sudan. The Za dynasty also figures in the early history of Islam in West Africa: tradition holds that one of its kings, Za Kusay, accepted Islam around the year 1010 after contact with Muslim merchants, making the Gao court one of the first in the region to adopt the new faith, though older beliefs and royal rituals remained strong for centuries.
pageData.para3: The dynasty's independence ended as the Mali Empire expanded east. In the early fourteenth century, the chronicles record, the Malian ruler Sakura, a former slave who had seized the throne of Mali, conquered Gao and reduced the Za kings to vassals around 1335. The Songhay remembered their subjugation, and in the next century, as Mali weakened, princes of the old line broke away. The chronicle names Ali Kulun and his brother as the founders of the restored Songhay state, the Sunni dynasty, whose greatest king Sunni Ali would build Gao into the capital of an empire.
pageData.para4: The Za dynasty matters because it shows that Songhay statehood was ancient long before the empire. Gao had been a seat of kings for six hundred years when Sunni Ali made it famous, and the Za rulers had already tied the middle Niger into the web of Saharan trade and introduced Islam to its court. The great mud-brick tomb known as the Tomb of Askia still rises over Gao, a monument of the imperial age that grew from these beginnings.
pageData.source2label: OpenStax World History: The People of the Sahel
pageData.source3label: OpenStax World History: The Songhai Empire
pageData.source4label: Black American History: The Za Dynasty Reigns in the Songhai Kingdom

pageData.title: The Mossi Kingdoms
pageData.titleline: The Mossi Kingdoms - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Mossi Kingdoms. The Mossi kingdoms (c. 1400-1896) were a group of related states in the bend of the Niger River, in what is now Burkina Faso, which for five centuries formed one of the most durable political systems of West Africa. Mossi tradition traces the kingdoms to a princess named Yennenga, daughter of a Dagomba king, whose son Ouedraogo became the ancestor of the Mossi rulers. From the fifteenth century, Mossi horsemen expanded over the Volta basin and founded a family of kingdoms, of which Ouagadougou, ruled by the Moro Naba, became the greatest.
pageData.para2: The Mossi state combined cavalry power with a remarkable social order. The Moro Naba and the kings of the lesser Mossi states, such as Yatenga, ruled through courts of titled officials, many of them drawn from the families of conquered peoples, while the original inhabitants kept authority over the earth as masters of the land. Mossi armies, famous for their mounted warriors, raided deep toward the Niger, clashing with the Songhai Empire and the Mali successor states, though they never built a large centralized empire of their own.
pageData.para3: The kingdoms long resisted both Islam and empire. Muslim merchants and clerics lived at the courts, but the Mossi kings generally kept their traditional religion, and Islam made only slow headway among the Mossi compared with their neighbors. When the great jihads of the nineteenth century swept across the Western Sudan, the Mossi states held their ground. Their independence finally ended with European conquest: French forces took Ouagadougou in 1896 and absorbed the kingdoms into what became the colony of Upper Volta.
pageData.para4: The Mossi legacy is still visible today. The Moro Naba of Ouagadougou remains an honored traditional ruler, and the Mossi language, Moore, is spoken by millions, making the Mossi the largest ethnic group in Burkina Faso. Historians value the Mossi kingdoms as a rare case of states that maintained their institutions, territory, and independence against empires, jihads, and slave raiders for nearly half a millennium.
pageData.source2label: Encyclopaedia Universalis: Royaume de Ouagadougou

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Butua and the Torwa Dynasty
pageData.titleline: The Kingdom of Butua and the Torwa Dynasty - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Butua and the Torwa Dynasty. The kingdom of Butua (c. 1450-1683), ruled by the Torwa dynasty, succeeded Great Zimbabwe as the leading Shona state of the southern African interior. When Great Zimbabwe was abandoned in the fifteenth century, political power shifted westward to the region the Portuguese called Butua, on the southwestern plateau of modern Zimbabwe. There the Torwa rulers built their capital at Khami, near modern Bulawayo, whose stone terraces and decorated walls are now a World Heritage site.
pageData.para2: Khami shows how the new kingdom adapted the old building traditions. Instead of the free-standing walls of Great Zimbabwe, the Torwa architects built revetted stone terraces rising in tiers up a hillside, faced with checkered and herringbone patterns, supporting the houses of the royal court. From Khami the Torwa mambo ruled the goldfields and cattle herds of the southwest, and trade goods reached his court from the Indian Ocean: Chinese porcelain, Portuguese glass beads, and other imports have been found in the ruins.
pageData.para3: The kingdom held its own in a violent age. In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries the Torwa rulers faced the rising power of the Mutapa state to the northeast and, beyond it, the Portuguese on the Zambezi and the coast. Butua's armies defeated at least one Portuguese-backed invasion, and the kingdom kept control of the gold trade routes running through its territory. Torwa power was finally broken in the 1680s, when the expanding Rozvi, led by the conqueror known as Changamire Dombo, defeated the Torwa and took over Butua.
pageData.para4: The Rozvi built on Torwa foundations, ruling from Khami and nearby Danangombe until the nineteenth century. The kingdom of Butua is remembered as the vital link between Great Zimbabwe and the later Shona states: it carried the stone-building tradition, the gold trade, and the political heritage of the Zimbabwe plateau through three centuries, and the ruins of Khami remain its most eloquent monument.

pageData.title: The Maravi Confederacy
pageData.titleline: The Maravi Confederacy - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Maravi Confederacy. The Maravi confederacy (c. 1480-1890) was a family of related states that dominated the lands south and west of Lake Malawi for four centuries. The ancestors of the Maravi peoples migrated into the region from the Congo basin, and oral traditions tell how their leaders, following a fiery comet or a sacred fire, established chiefdoms around the lake and the Shire valley. By the sixteenth century a Maravi ruler known as the Kalonga, based among the Chewa of central Malawi, had built the greatest of these states, while related dynasties ruled the Nyanja and Mang'anja peoples further south.
pageData.para2: The confederacy's wealth rested on trade and tribute. Maravi chiefs controlled the routes carrying ivory, and later enslaved people, from the interior to the Swahili and Portuguese traders of the Mozambique coast, and their authority reached at its height from the Luangwa River to the Indian Ocean. The Kalonga's court was a ritual center as much as a political one: sacred fire was carried from his capital to install new chiefs, and rainmaking and ancestral cults underpinned royal power. The Portuguese, arriving in the seventeenth century, dealt with the Maravi state as the principal power of the region.
pageData.para3: From the eighteenth century the confederacy weakened. Trade routes shifted, regional chiefs such as Undi and Mwase asserted their independence, and the nineteenth century brought devastating new pressures: slave raiding, Yao migrations from the east, and finally the arrival of the Ngoni, southern African warriors fleeing the wars of Shaka's time, who overran much of the Maravi world. By the 1890s the British had established the protectorate of Nyasaland over the old Maravi lands.
pageData.para4: The Maravi states are the ancestors of modern Malawi, whose name comes from the confederacy itself. The Chewa, Nyanja, and related peoples still make up most of the population of Malawi and eastern Zambia, and their chiefs, language, and traditions of kingship descend directly from the states built by the Kalonga and his kin half a millennium ago.
pageData.source2label: Wiley Encyclopedia of Empire: Maravi Kingdom

pageData.title: The Sultanate of Agadez
pageData.titleline: The Sultanate of Agadez - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Sultanate of Agadez. The sultanate of Agadez (c. 1449-1900) was a Tuareg state of the Air mountains in what is now northern Niger, which for four and a half centuries guarded one of the great crossroads of the Sahara. The town of Agadez had long been a caravan stop where routes from the Sudan met the road to Tripoli and Egypt. Around 1449, according to tradition, the Tuareg tribes of Air agreed to accept a sultan of their own, and a prince connected to the Songhay ruling family, Ilisawan, was installed as the first of a long line.
pageData.para2: The sultanate's lifeblood was the desert trade. Agadez stood at the junction of the routes from Kano and Hausaland in the south to Ghat, Ghadames, and Tripoli in the north, and caravans of thousands of camels passed through with salt from the desert mines of Bilma and Taoudenni, gold, kola nuts, leather, and enslaved people. The sultans taxed the trade, protected the caravans, and balanced between the great powers of the region: the Songhai Empire, which claimed Agadez until its fall in 1591, the Ottoman regency of Tripoli, the Bornu Empire, and later the Sokoto Caliphate.
pageData.para3: The city they ruled became a monument of Saharan architecture. Its great mosque, rebuilt in its present form in the nineteenth century, carries a mud-brick minaret some 27 meters high, the tallest of its kind in the world, and the old town around it, with its earthen houses and narrow lanes, is now a World Heritage site. German explorer Heinrich Barth, who reached Agadez in 1850, described a still-imposing town at the head of the caravan roads.
pageData.para4: The sultanate's long independence ended with the European conquest of the Sahara. French forces occupied Agadez around 1900, faced fierce Tuareg resistance during the revolt of 1916-17, and incorporated Air into the colony of Niger. Yet the sultanate survives as a traditional institution: the Sultan of Agadez is still enthroned today, a living heir of the state that ruled the crossroads of the central Sahara for four centuries.

pageData.title: The Daju and Tunjur Kingdoms
pageData.titleline: The Daju and Tunjur Kingdoms - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Daju and Tunjur Kingdoms. The Daju and Tunjur kingdoms (c. 1200-1650) were the successive powers that ruled Darfur, the western Sudanese region between the Nile and Lake Chad, before the rise of the famous Keira sultanate. The Daju, a people of the Jebel Marra mountains, are remembered in Darfur tradition as the earliest historical kings of the region. Their rulers built stone-faced palaces and strongholds in the mountains, the ruins of which can still be seen, and they controlled the desert-edge trade routes linking the Nile valley with the lands to the west.
pageData.para2: According to the traditions collected by historians, the Daju kings were overthrown by the Tunjur, a people of mixed origins who migrated into Darfur from the northwest. The Tunjur ruled from mountain capitals such as Uri and Turra in Jebel Marra, and they developed ties with the Islamic world: Tunjur sultans corresponded with Muslim rulers, built mosques, and adopted the title of sultan, while governing a population of farmers and cattle herders through a court of titled officials.
pageData.para3: The Tunjur in turn gave way in the seventeenth century to the Keira dynasty of the Fur people. Tradition credits a leader named Sulayman Solong, remembered as the founder of the Fur sultanate, with defeating the last Tunjur king and establishing Keira rule around 1650. Under the Keira sultans, Darfur became a major Muslim state trading with Egypt, but the memory of the earlier kingdoms was carefully preserved in Fur royal ceremonies and in the genealogies that linked the new dynasty to its predecessors.
pageData.para4: The Daju and Tunjur kingdoms matter because they reveal the deep roots of statehood in the Sudanese Sahel. Long before the better-documented sultanates, mountain and desert peoples of Darfur were building fortified capitals, organizing kingdoms, and joining the caravan networks of the Sahara and the Nile. Their ruined strongholds in Jebel Marra, and the traditions that preserve their names, are among the few witnesses to five centuries of history in one of Africa's least-known regions.

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Kaffa
pageData.titleline: The Kingdom of Kaffa - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Kaffa. The kingdom of Kaffa (c. 1390-1897) was a powerful state of the rainforested highlands of southwestern Ethiopia, famous as the homeland of coffee. The Kafficho people trace their kings to a dynasty called the Minjo, and traditions recorded by the royal chroniclers tell how early kings such as Minjilo consolidated the highland plateau behind great natural defenses. Kaffa was protected by deep river gorges and dense forest, and its rulers sealed the few passes with guarded gates, keeping the kingdom independent and mysterious to outsiders for centuries.
pageData.para2: The kingdom grew rich on trade and on its extraordinary natural endowment. Kaffa exported gold, ivory, civet musk, slaves, and above all coffee, which grows wild in its mountain forests and was carried north along ancient trade routes to the Ethiopian highlands and beyond. The Kaffa king, or tato, ruled from capitals such as Bonga through a hierarchy of appointed officials, and his authority was sacred as well as political. A finely organized system of districts, tribute, and royal estates supported the court.
pageData.para3: Kaffa's seclusion could not last forever. In the nineteenth century the expanding Ethiopian Empire pushed south under Emperor Menelik II, and after a hard campaign the royal army conquered Kaffa in 1897. The last king, Gaki Sherocho, was captured and sent into captivity, and his kingdom was absorbed into Ethiopia as a province. The old capital at Bonga dwindled, though the Kafficho people and their language remain a living community of the southwest.
pageData.para4: The kingdom's most famous legacy is botanical. The wild arabica coffee that still grows in the Kafa forests is the ancestor of much of the world's coffee, and the very name of the plant is commonly traced to the kingdom. The Kafa Biosphere Reserve now protects those mountain rainforests, a reminder that the little-known kingdom of Kaffa gave the world one of its most beloved crops.
